intemperance.definition: lack of moderation, especially in drinking
sentences: His intemperance cost him a liver, a marriage, and eventually a knighthood.
Intemperance in argument loses more cases than weak evidence does.

intend.definition: to plan or mean to do
sentences: He intended the remark kindly, which the transcript entirely failed to convey.
The road to trouble is paved with things people intended to do on Monday.
Two weeks of intensive study beat six months of the leisurely kind.
Intensive farming produces more per acre and fewer birds per hedgerow.
He was interred in a village churchyard beside a rival he had outlived by a week.
The report was interred in an appendix and never exhumed.

interchangeable.definition: able to be swapped without difference
sentences: The parts are interchangeable, which is why the repair took nine minutes.
The candidates' policies were interchangeable and their accents were not.
The court interdicted the sale pending a full valuation.
Naval patrols interdicted the shipments and quadrupled the price.
An intermediary carried messages between two people in the same building.
Removing the intermediary saves a fee and loses a translator.
The interminable introduction outlasted two audience members and one microphone battery.
Interminable means literally without end, which is how the meeting felt at hour three.
Intermittent faults are the worst kind: they vanish whenever an engineer arrives.
Intermittent rain ruined the match without ever stopping it.

internecine.definition: destructive to both sides within a group
sentences: Internecine feuding cost the party three elections and one entire generation.
Internecine conflict is the only kind where both sides can lose completely.

interplay.definition: the way things affect each other
sentences: The interplay of light and shadow does more work in that film than the dialogue.
Policy is the interplay of intention and whatever the ministry can actually implement.

interpolate.definition: to insert something between existing parts
sentences: A later scribe interpolated three lines that theologians argued over for centuries.
You interpolate between known points and extrapolate beyond them, at your own risk.

interregnum.definition: a gap between two reigns or governments
sentences: During the interregnum, three deputies each behaved as though they had been chosen.
The interregnum lasted eight months and produced the department's best work.
The two families' fortunes were intertwined through four generations and one lawsuit.
Their careers were intertwined so tightly that neither could be described alone.
He intimated that funds might be found, and nothing was ever written down.
The verb intimates; the adjective is close and private. Same spelling, different stress.
The first intimation of trouble was a supplier asking to be paid in advance.
There was no intimation in the letter of what the meeting would actually decide.
The problem was intractable for forty years and then dissolved in one paper.
An intractable colleague is more expensive than an incompetent one.
Both sides were intransigent, which is why the mediator lasted nine days.
Intransigence is principle when you agree with it and obstruction when you do not.
The intrepid reporter filed from a rooftop with a satellite phone and a bad cough.
Intrepid means not trembling, which is a lower bar than it sounds.
Court intrigue consumed more energy than governing ever did.
The department's intrigue was conducted entirely by calendar invitation.
The problem is intrinsic to the design and no amount of training will fix it.
Intrinsic motivation outlasts every bonus scheme ever invented.
A week of introspection produced one useful decision and four abandoned ones.
Introspection is unreliable evidence about a mind and the only evidence available.
The office was inundated with applications and staffed by two people.
The river inundated the water meadows, which is what water meadows are for.
Ten years of night shifts inured him to a schedule nobody else could survive.
You can be inured to bad news and still notice when it changes.
Inured to rejection, she submitted the manuscript for the twenty-third time.
Nurses grow inured to the sights and never to the families.
The invasive species arrived in ballast water and rewrote the whole lake.
Invasive questions at an interview reveal more about the interviewer.
The letter descended into invective by the second paragraph and never recovered.
Invective is the sound of an argument that has run out of arguments.

inveigle.definition: to persuade by flattery or deceit
sentences: He inveigled his way onto the guest list with a name that resembled someone important's.
She inveigled two colleagues into a project neither had time for.
The investiture took forty minutes and the actual handover took a year.
Investiture disputes between kings and popes shaped medieval Europe more than most battles.
An inveterate note-taker, he filled sixty notebooks and read none of them twice.
Inveterate liars are undone by memory, not by conscience.

invidious.definition: likely to cause resentment; unfairly discriminating
sentences: Ranking colleagues publicly puts the manager in an invidious position.
The invidious comparison to her predecessor followed her for a decade.
A cold walk invigorated a discussion that had died indoors.
New funding invigorated a department that had been coasting since 2011.

inviolable.definition: never to be broken or violated
sentences: The inviolable rule about Sunday lunch survived three house moves and one divorce.
Diplomatic immunity treats an embassy as inviolable, which occasionally strains everyone's patience.
The seal remained inviolate for four hundred years and eleven minutes.
His privacy stayed inviolate until the biography arrived.

invocation.definition: an appeal to authority or a higher power
sentences: The invocation of national security ended the questioning immediately.
The ceremony opened with an invocation nobody under forty could follow.

invoke.definition: to call on for support or authority
sentences: He invoked a precedent from 1931 that turned out to have been overturned in 1932.
To invoke tradition is to hope nobody looks up when it started.
The explanation was too involved to fit in the summary, which is usually a warning.
She was involved in four projects and finishing none of them.
He believed his position invulnerable right up until the audit began.
Achilles was invulnerable except at one tendon, which is now a proverb.
The irascible chef ran the best kitchen and the highest staff turnover in the city.
Irascible before coffee and merely difficult after it.
The parking policy drew the ire of everyone who had ever owned a car.
Ire is short, old, and much loved by headline writers for exactly that reason.
It irked him that the correction never received the attention the error had.
Small things irk; large things enrage. The small ones do more cumulative damage.
The irksome requirement to log every hour produced logs nobody ever read.
An irksome colleague is survivable; an irksome commute is not.
The ironclad guarantee had one exception, and it was the one that occurred.
An ironclad alibi is generally the most suspicious kind.

irony.definition: an outcome contrary to what was expected
sentences: The irony of the fire station burning down was noted by absolutely everyone.
Irony survives translation badly, which is why treaties avoid it.
The logic was irrefutable and the premise was invented.
Irrefutable evidence still requires somebody willing to look at it.
An irresolute leader is worse in a crisis than a wrong one.
He stood irresolute in the doorway until the decision made itself.
The irreverent obituary was the only one the family actually liked.
Irreverent humor is the immune system of an institution.
The transfer was irrevocable, as the terms had said in a font nobody read.
Very few decisions are truly irrevocable, and those are worth a second night's sleep.

issue.definition: to send out or publish officially
sentences: The ministry issued a denial that raised more questions than the story had.
Passports are issued in four weeks and, in emergencies, in four hours.

itinerant.definition: traveling from place to place for work
sentences: An itinerant teacher covered six villages and slept in a different one each night.
Itinerant work suits the young and punishes everyone else.

itinerary.definition: a planned route or travel schedule
sentences: The itinerary allowed eleven minutes between two airports in different cities.
A good itinerary is mostly the things you decided to leave out.

itinerate.definition: to travel from place to place
sentences: Preachers itinerated between market towns, drawing crowds and complaints in equal number.
He itinerated for a decade and then bought a shop.
The jargon exists to save time among specialists and to exclude everyone else.
Strip the jargon and the memo said: we don't know yet.

jaundice.definition: bitterness or prejudice; a yellowing condition
sentences: Twenty years in the industry left him with a jaundice toward every press release.
The jaundiced eye sees corruption in every coincidence.
The jejune conclusion undid three chapters of genuinely careful work.
Jejune comes from a Latin word for fasting: the writing is undernourished.
Publishing early would jeopardize the patent, so the paper waited eleven months.
One careless sentence jeopardized four years of quiet negotiation.
Her jet hair in the portrait is the only thing the restorer did not touch.
Jet is a fossilized wood, which is why jet-black is a mineral color.
The plan jettisoned its most interesting feature to satisfy a regulator's footnote.
Ships jettison cargo to stay afloat, which is where the word and the wisdom come from.

jibe.definition: to agree or be consistent with
sentences: His story did not jibe with the timestamps, which ended the interview.
As a noun it is a taunt; as a verb, agreement. English enjoys this sort of thing.
The editorial's jingoism embarrassed the paper within a decade.
Jingoism comes from a music-hall song, which is a fittingly cheap origin.
The jingoist demanded a war he had no intention of attending.
Every jingoist is certain he speaks for a silent, agreeing nation.
His jocular tone at the disciplinary hearing was a serious miscalculation.
A jocular aside can carry a criticism that a direct one could not.
Wordsworth found the daffodils jocund, which is a lot to ask of a flower.
The jocund mood at breakfast did not survive the agenda.
The jovial doorman knew four hundred names and every one of the dogs.
Jovial comes from Jupiter, whose astrological influence was supposed to make you cheerful.
Jubilant supporters filled a square that had been empty an hour earlier.
The jubilant press release was withdrawn when the result was recounted.
A judicious edit removed the one paragraph that would have caused a lawsuit.
Judicious silence has saved more careers than eloquence.
The retail juggernaut opened four hundred stores and closed a thousand smaller ones.
The word comes from a temple cart said to crush those in its path.
At this juncture, the polite phrase for right now, the money ran out.
The company reached a juncture where doing nothing was the most expensive option.

junket.definition: a trip taken at someone else's expense
sentences: The fact-finding junket found four facts and one very good beach.
Journalists on a junket rarely write anything the host will regret.

junta.definition: a military group ruling after seizing power
sentences: The junta promised elections within a year and held them within eleven.
A junta always announces that it acted reluctantly, and always at dawn.

justify.definition: to show to be right or reasonable
sentences: The results justified a method that had looked reckless for two years.
If you have to justify it three times, it may not be justified.

juxtapose.definition: to place side by side for contrast
sentences: The exhibit juxtaposes the sketch and the finished work, to the sketch's advantage.
Juxtaposing the two budgets made the argument without a word of commentary.
A keen observer noticed that the shadows in the photograph fell two ways.
He was keen to start and keener still to be finished.

kindle.definition: to start a fire or arouse feeling
sentences: One good teacher kindled an interest that lasted fifty years.
It takes dry wood to kindle a fire and dry facts to kindle an argument.
The sculpture is kinetic, which means the museum employs someone to oil it.
Her kinetic style of teaching left the front row exhausted.

knack.definition: a natural skill or clever trick
sentences: She had a knack for asking the question that unlocked the whole interview.
There is a knack to the door, which the landlord mentions only after you move in.

knell.definition: a sound signaling the end of something
sentences: The supplier's withdrawal sounded the knell for the whole project.
A knell is a bell rung slowly, which is why the metaphor is so heavy.

knight.definition: to confer an honorary title on
sentences: He was knighted for services to a charity he had joined the previous year.
Being knighted changes the name on the letters and nothing else whatsoever.
They picnicked on a knoll with a view of the road they had escaped.
One grassy knoll has done more for conspiracy theories than any document.
He refused to kowtow to a board that had never read the research.
Kowtowing began as a literal forehead-to-floor bow at the Chinese court.
Kudos went to the department that announced the work, not the one that did it.
Kudos is singular in Greek, which has not stopped anyone.
Once labeled difficult, she found every disagreement read as proof.
Labeling a problem is often mistaken for solving it.

labor.definition: to work hard; to belabor a point
sentences: He labored the analogy until it collapsed under its own weight.
They labored for six months on a report the minister read in the car.
The laborious transcription took a year and revealed one crucial sentence.
His laborious prose is the sound of someone working very hard in the wrong direction.
The review lacerated the book and made its author famous.
Barbed wire lacerated the coat and, eventually, the argument for shortcuts.
The lachrymose finale had the audience reaching for handkerchiefs and the critics for adjectives.
Lachrymose comes from the Latin for tear, which the word does look like.
A lackluster first half was followed by a second half that was worse.
Lackluster literally means without shine, which is a kinder way to say boring.
Asked to describe the disaster, the laconic engineer said only: "It fell."
Sparta was so laconic that a threat of invasion drew a one-word reply: "If."
The laggards in the adoption curve turned out to have been right to wait.
One laggard on a group hike sets the pace for everyone.
He lambasted the plan in public and adopted it in November.
Lambast and lambaste are the same word arguing about a silent E.
The auditors lambasted a process that three previous audits had merely noted.
Being lambasted in the trade press did the company less harm than the silence before it.
Editors have lamented the decline of attention since roughly the invention of print.
He lamented the loss of the old building while approving its replacement.
The cartoon lampooned all four candidates and offended only the one it flattered.
Being lampooned is the surest evidence of having arrived.
The lancet gave the medical journal its name and its founder's reputation for sharpness.
A lancet window is tall, narrow, and pointed like the blade.

landmark.definition: a decisive event or notable feature
sentences: The ruling was a landmark and, for eleven years, entirely unenforced.
The pub is a landmark for everyone except the map, which omits it.
A languid afternoon in August produced nothing except the idea for the whole book.
Her languid delivery made every sentence sound like a favor.

languish.definition: to grow weak or be neglected
sentences: The proposal languished in a drawer for four years and passed in a week.
He languished on the waiting list while healthier people were seen faster.

lapidary.definition: elegantly concise, as if carved in stone
sentences: Her lapidary style fits an argument into a sentence you cannot forget.
Lapidary prose is written for stone, which is why it survives paper.
Petty larceny in the stockroom cost less than the surveillance system installed to stop it.
Grand larceny is petty larceny with a higher price tag on the item.
The larder held four jars of chutney and no explanation for any of them.
A well-stocked larder is the difference between a storm and an inconvenience.
The department survived on the largess of one alumnus and the fear of losing it.
Political largess before an election is called investment and after it, a deficit.
His largesse funded the wing, the chair, and the plaque listing his largesse.
Largesse from the powerful always arrives with an unspoken invoice.
The lascivious remark was reported, denied, and confirmed by the recording.
Lascivious material in the eighteenth century would now barely qualify as flirtation.
A general lassitude settled over the office in the third week of August.
Lassitude after a crisis is the body sending an invoice.
The latent demand appeared the moment the price dropped four percent.
Latent talent stays latent without somebody willing to notice it.

latitude.definition: freedom to act as one chooses
sentences: Junior staff were given latitude on method and none at all on deadline.
The contract allowed latitude that the client had not intended to grant.
The obituaries lauded a career whose difficult middle decade went unmentioned.
He was lauded abroad and audited at home, in the same month.
The aim was laudable and the execution was a catastrophe.
"Laudable effort" in a review means the result was not.
The lavish launch party cost more than the product's first year of revenue.
He was lavish with praise and extremely careful with credit.
Lax security meant the door had been propped open since March.
Lax standards do not fail immediately, which is exactly the problem.
Explaining it to a layperson forced him to discover he did not understand it either.
The jury is twelve laypersons deciding what four experts could not agree on.
The two firms were in league long before the merger was announced.
A league was also three miles, which is why old maps are so confusing.
Investors were leery of a forecast that assumed nothing would ever go wrong.
He was leery of anyone who agreed with him immediately.
Accounting legerdemain moved the loss into a subsidiary nobody consolidated.
Legerdemain is French for "light of hand," which is a generous name for cheating.
The lethargic response to the first warning made the second one inevitable.
A heavy lunch makes a lethargic afternoon, which every scheduler ignores.

levee.definition: an embankment holding back a river
sentences: The levee held for two days and failed at the one point nobody had inspected.
Building the levee higher moved the flooding downstream to a poorer parish.

level.definition: to direct an accusation; to make flat
sentences: Serious charges were leveled at a department that had already been abolished.
The storm leveled the fence and left the greenhouse untouched.
A moment of levity at the funeral was exactly what the family needed.
Levity in a crisis is either leadership or negligence, depending on the timing.

levy.definition: to impose a tax or fine
sentences: The council levied a charge on empty properties and halved the number of them.
Taxes are levied; the resentment is voluntary.
Johnson called lexicography harmless drudgery, which was false modesty and mostly accurate.
Modern lexicography records how words are used, not how they ought to be.

liability.definition: a legal obligation or a disadvantage
sentences: His candor was an asset in research and a liability in negotiation.
The liability was capped at the contract value, which the lawyers noticed and the client did not.
He was liberal with other people's time and careful with his own.
A liberal interpretation of the rules kept everyone employed and nobody safe.
Automating the report liberated four hours a week that immediately filled with meetings.
The town was liberated twice in one month by opposing armies.
The libertine of the memoirs turns out, in the letters, to have been rather lonely.
A libertine in one decade is merely fashionable in the next.
The libretto is silly and the music has carried it for two centuries.
Librettists get one line in the program and none of the applause.
The licentious court was described in detail by chroniclers who clearly enjoyed the research.
Licentious originally meant simply unlicensed, which is a mild beginning for the word.
The first draft was cut by half; the second was likewise treated.
"Likewise" is the standard reply of someone who did not catch what you said.
Her limpid prose explains quantum mechanics without a single equation.
The limpid pool was four feet deeper than it looked, as limpid pools are.

lineament.definition: a distinctive feature, especially of a face
sentences: The lineaments of the old policy are visible in every line of the new one.
The portrait captures his lineaments and none of his manner.
London lionized him for one season and forgot him during the next.
To be lionized is to be admired by people who have not read the work.
The lissome dancer made the difficult sequence look like a decision rather than a feat.
Lissome is lithesome with the middle worn away.
A listless second half emptied the stands before the final whistle.
He was listless for a month and then, without explanation, entirely himself.
The complaint was a litany of small grievances stretching back eleven years.
A litany in church is a prayer; in an argument it is exhausting.

litigation.definition: the process of taking legal action
sentences: Six years of litigation cost more than the disputed contract was ever worth.
The threat of litigation settles more disputes than litigation does.

livelihood.definition: the means of earning a living
sentences: The closure removed the livelihood of half a village in a single announcement.
He turned a hobby into a livelihood and lost the hobby in the process.
She was livid about the leak and icily polite for the entire meeting.
Livid also means bluish-grey, which is the color of a bruise and, apparently, of rage.
He was loath to admit the earlier estimate had been invented.
Loath is reluctant; loathe is to hate. The E does all the work.
She loathed the phrase "circle back" and used it four times that afternoon.
He loathed the work and did it beautifully for thirty years.

lode.definition: a rich source or vein of ore
sentences: The archive proved a lode of material nobody had thought to mine.
The lode ran out in 1904 and the town emptied within a decade.

lofty.definition: elevated in position or ideals; haughty
sentences: The lofty aims of the charter were reduced to a car parking policy by June.
His lofty tone at the meeting cost him the vote he was certain of.
She logged every call, which is why the inquiry took four days instead of four months.
Ships log their speed with an actual log on a rope, which is where the word comes from.
The loquacious taxi driver delivered a complete history of the city in nine minutes.
Loquacious witnesses give away what careful ones protect.
A pair of louts ruined an evening that four hundred other people had enjoyed.
The lout at the back of the bus is a permanent feature of urban life.
His lucid explanation of the tax change was the only useful thing on the news.
She had lucid intervals in which she named every visitor correctly.
The lucrative side business quietly became the main one.
Lucrative work and interesting work occasionally overlap, usually by accident.
His lugubrious delivery made the good news sound like a diagnosis.
The lugubrious hound in the painting is doing most of the emotional work.
In the lull between the two waves, everyone assumed it was over.
The lull in the storm is when experienced sailors do the most work.
The old bus lumbered up the hill at a speed that permitted conversation.
The process lumbers along and arrives, eventually, at the same place.
Four luminaries were invited and one turned up, brilliantly.
Every field has luminaries who publish and workhorses who make the results replicate.
The luminous dial had been painted with radium, which killed the women who painted it.
Her luminous performance made a thin script feel like literature.
The lurid details filled four pages and the correction filled one paragraph.
Lurid was originally a sickly yellow, which the tabloids have improved upon.
The luxuriant garden was the result of total neglect and excellent drainage.
Luxuriant is abundant growth; luxurious is expensive comfort.
The museum's macabre collection is its most visited and least photographed room.
Macabre humor is how emergency workers survive their own week.
They machinated for a year to remove a director who resigned voluntarily anyway.
To machinate is to run a machine of plots, which is exactly how it feels.
The machination required six people to keep one secret, which is five too many.
Every reorganization is explained as strategy and remembered as machination.
The machinations behind the appointment took four months and one leaked email to unravel.
History remembers the machinations and forgets who did the actual work.
The madrigal group met on Tuesdays and disagreed about tempo for thirty years.
Madrigals are polyphonic, which means everyone is singing something slightly different on purpose.

maelstrom.definition: a violent whirlpool or turbulent situation
sentences: He walked into a maelstrom of accusations that had been building for months.
The original Maelstrom is a real current off Norway that terrified real sailors.
The magisterial three-volume history has not been superseded in fifty years.
His magisterial tone worked in the lecture hall and failed completely at home.
Magnanimity in victory costs nothing and buys the next decade.
His magnanimity extended to everyone except the one critic who had been right.

magnanimous.definition: generous and forgiving, especially to rivals
sentences: The magnanimous concession speech was the best thing he ever wrote.
Being magnanimous when you have lost is much harder and much rarer.
The shipping magnate endowed a library and named it after his mother.
Every magnate's biography contains one chapter that the lawyers shortened.

maintain.definition: to assert firmly; to keep in condition
sentences: He maintained his innocence for eleven years and was proved right in the twelfth.
Maintaining the building cost more than building it had.
A majority of one is still a majority, and it governed for four years.
The silent majority is silent partly because nobody has asked it anything.
The makeshift repair lasted nineteen years, which embarrassed the engineers who costed the real one.
A makeshift solution becomes permanent the moment it works twice.
The maladroit apology managed to insult two more people.
Maladroit is French for badly-right-handed, which is unkind on several fronts.
Short-termism is the malady of every organization judged quarterly.
The malady was diagnosed correctly in 1931 and treated correctly in 1954.

malaise.definition: a general feeling of unease or discontent
sentences: A malaise settled over the industry that no single figure explained.
Malaise is what a doctor writes when the patient is unwell and the tests are not.

malapropism.definition: a comic misuse of a similar-sounding word
sentences: "Dance a flamingo" is a malapropism that has entered the family permanently.
Mrs. Malaprop in the play gave her name to a lifetime of accidental comedy.
Management dismissed them as malcontents, and the malcontents turned out to be right.
Every organization labels its early warning system a group of malcontents.
He left the meeting with a malediction that the minutes recorded as "comments."
Malediction is bad-speaking; benediction is good-speaking. Both were once thought to work.
The malevolent rumor was traced to one anonymous account and four willing repeaters.
Most harm is careless rather than malevolent, which is somehow less comforting.
The inquiry found malfeasance at three levels and prosecuted at none.
Malfeasance is doing the wrong thing; nonfeasance is doing nothing at all.
The verdict required proof of malice, which the emails supplied abundantly.
Never attribute to malice what incompetence explains, but do not rule it out either.

malign.definition: to speak evil of; to slander
sentences: He was maligned for a decade and rehabilitated in an appendix.
The much-maligned regulation turned out to have prevented two disasters.

malinger.definition: to fake illness to avoid work
sentences: He was accused of malingering and diagnosed, three weeks later, with something serious.
Malingering is a real problem and a much-abused accusation.

malingerer.definition: one who fakes illness to avoid duty
sentences: The sergeant treated everyone as a malingerer until the third case of pneumonia.
One malingerer costs a team less than a manager who suspects everyone.
Gold is malleable enough to be beaten into a sheet you can see through.
A malleable committee is convenient for exactly as long as you are the one shaping it.
The malodorous fridge united a hostile office in a single afternoon.
Malodorous is what a report says when "stinks" is unavailable.
The debt manacled the company to a supplier it could not afford to leave.
The prisoner was manacled for a hearing about a parking offense.
The unfairness was manifest to everyone except the committee that designed it.
The disagreement became manifest only when the budget arrived.
The strike was a manifestation of a grievance nobody had bothered to record.
Rust is the manifestation; the water got in years ago.
His mannered delivery divided audiences into devotees and deserters.
The mannered prose of the period reads now like everyone was performing.
He manumitted eleven people in his will and none during his life.
The word means "to send from the hand," which is precisely the gesture of release.
A single typo on the cover marred an otherwise flawless edition.
The evening was marred by a speech that had been warned against twice.
Gulls marauded the picnic with a coordination that suggested planning.
Marauding bands took the harvest and left the seed corn, which was strategic.
The improvement was marginal and the press release was not.
Marginal seats decide elections, which is why they get all the new roads.

marginalize.definition: to push to the edges of importance
sentences: The reorganization marginalized a team that had produced most of the revenue.
You can marginalize a person without ever saying a word to them.

martial.definition: relating to war or the military
sentences: Martial law was declared at midnight and lifted, quietly, four years later.
His martial bearing came from twelve years in a band, not an army.
The martinet in charge of scheduling ran the only department that never missed a deadline.
Martinet was a French drillmaster whose name became a complaint.
Gladstone reportedly masticated every mouthful thirty-two times, which cannot have improved conversation.
The machine masticates the waste into a pulp nobody wants to look at.

matriarch.definition: a woman who heads a family or group
sentences: The matriarch settled disputes at Sunday lunch and nowhere else.
Elephant herds are led by a matriarch whose memory of water holes keeps everyone alive.
Two glasses in, he became maudlin about a school he had disliked intensely.
The maudlin final scene undoes an hour of restraint.
The reviewers mauled the first act and praised the second.
The bear did not maul the tent; it removed it entirely.
He maundered through twenty minutes of anecdote before reaching the agenda.
Maundering in a memoir is charming; in a meeting it is theft.
The maverick of the department was right twice and unemployable by the third time.
Samuel Maverick refused to brand his cattle, which is how unbranded people got his name.
The mawkish tribute video made even the honoree wince.
Mawkish once meant nauseating, which explains what too much sentiment does.
"Measure twice, cut once" is a maxim that has saved more wood than skill has.
Every maxim has a contradicting maxim, which is why judgment still exists.
The conversation meandered for an hour and arrived somewhere neither had expected.
Rivers meander because water is lazy in a very precise way.

mediate.definition: to intervene to settle a dispute
sentences: She mediated between two departments that had communicated only by memo for a year.
To mediate you must be trusted by people who trust nobody.
A pleasant melancholy settles over the coast in late September.
Melancholy was once a medical diagnosis involving black bile and no evidence.
The exhibition is a melange of three collections and no discernible argument.
Dinner was a melange of what four households had left in their fridges.
The melee at the gate lasted four minutes and dominated the coverage for a week.
In the melee somebody's shoe was lost and never claimed.
His mellifluous voice made even the safety announcements sound like poetry.
Mellifluous literally means flowing with honey, which is a fair description of a good broadcaster.
The cell membrane decides what enters, which makes it the busiest doorman in biology.
A thin membrane of politeness separated the two factions at dinner.
The mendacious prospectus described a factory that had never been built.
A mendacious witness is easier to handle than a sincerely mistaken one.
The mendacity was not in the numbers but in the sentence introducing them.
Mendacity ages badly, because records outlive memories.

mendicant.definition: a beggar, especially a religious one
sentences: Mendicant orders owned nothing and organized everything.
The mendicant at the cathedral door had been there longer than the current bishop.
His motives were mercenary and his results were excellent, which complicated the moral.
A mercenary interest in the outcome is not the same as a corrupt one, quite.
The mercurial director was adored on set and unemployable between films.
Mercury the god was quick and Mercury the metal will not stay still either.
The meretricious charm of the prospectus survived exactly one site visit.
Meretricious comes from a word for a prostitute, which is harsh on the profession and the prose.
The proposal has merit and no chance, which is a common combination.
Promotion on merit requires somebody willing to define merit before the vacancy.

meritocracy.definition: rule by those judged most able
sentences: The word meritocracy was coined as satire and adopted as a compliment.
Every meritocracy eventually has to explain why the same families keep qualifying.
The medal is for meritorious service, which usually means twenty unglamorous years.
A meritorious argument still loses to a well-connected one.
The plot mesmerized viewers who could not have summarized a minute of it.
Franz Mesmer hypnotized Vienna and left his name behind when the theory collapsed.
The pilot project metamorphosed into a department of ninety within four years.
A caterpillar metamorphoses by dissolving almost entirely, which is a lot to ask of anyone.
The building's metamorphosis from mill to museum took nine years and three architects.
Kafka's Metamorphosis begins with the transformation and spends the rest on the family.
He said the department was on fire in the metaphorical sense, twice, before anyone checked.
Most everyday language is metaphorical and has forgotten that it is.

metaphysical.definition: concerning abstract reality beyond the physical
sentences: The dispute turned metaphysical, which meant no experiment could settle it.
The metaphysical poets compared love to compasses and got away with it.
Her meteoric rise took eleven years, which nobody mentions in the profile.
Meteoric ought to imply falling and burning up, which the metaphor cheerfully ignores.
